title: Choosing a collector and what System.gc() means

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A latency-critical service runs on a heap of several hundred gigabytes and needs GC pauses below one millisecond. Which collector fits?

options.text: ZGC, whose concurrent work keeps pauses short however large the heap is.
options.says: ZGC is concurrent, with sub-millisecond pauses that scale to terabyte heaps, which is exactly this requirement.

options.text: Parallel GC, whose many threads keep pauses short however large the heap is.
options.says: Parallel GC stops the application for each collection and aims at throughput, so its pauses grow with the heap.

options.text: G1 GC, whose regions keep pauses short however large the heap is.
options.says: G1 balances throughput and latency with pause targets far above one millisecond on a heap this size.

questions.stem: After clearing a large cache, code calls System.gc(). What does that call do?

options.text: It runs a full collection, and returns when that collection has finished.
options.says: The call is a request, not a command, so nothing guarantees a collection has happened when it returns.

options.text: It asks the JVM for a collection, and the JVM decides whether to run one.
options.says: System.gc() is a hint; the JVM may ignore it (and -XX:+DisableExplicitGC turns it off), and when honoured it usually triggers a full GC.

options.text: It clears the objects the caller has set to null, and keeps the others.
options.says: The collector decides when, what and how to collect by reachability; a caller cannot aim it at particular objects.

concepts: Parallel GC maximises throughput, G1 balances latency and throughput as the default, and ZGC keeps pauses under a millisecond on huge heaps.
System.gc() is only a request the JVM may ignore, and when honoured it usually means a costly full collection.
